clue.text: Popular goalie welcomes new local manager

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so the popular goalie pair opens up to let a letter inside

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
a goalkeeper is a keeper

explanation.surface: A well-liked goalkeeper greets a newly appointed local team boss.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang the 'local' is one's neighbourhood pub, so its manager is the person who runs it.
explanation.definitionFit: A local is a British pub, and the person who runs a pub or inn is its landlord, the classic innkeeper.

clue.text: Camping without sibling can be demanding

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the camping phrase sits around the sibling

parts.note: camping is being in a tent, written as one run of letters
sis is short for sister, a sibling

explanation.surface: A child whining that a camping trip without their brother or sister is a real chore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is read in its old sense of 'outside', not 'lacking', so the camping phrase is split around the sibling.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone insistent keeps pressing their demands, so the adjective is a straight synonym of demanding.

clue.text: Woman who forced my mum out of her first home

definitions.text: Woman who forced my mum out of her first home

parts.words: Woman who forced my mum out of her first home
parts.note: a mother's first home is her own mother's womb, and the woman who pushed her out of it in childbirth is the speaker's grandmother

explanation.surface: Sounds like a family feud: some woman evicted my mother from her first house.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'first home' is the womb, and being 'forced out' is being born, so the woman is my mum's mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanna is a familiar British word for a grandmother, the mother of one's mum.

clue.text: Vitally important I must stop awful lateness

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so the single letter is pushed into the middle of the jumbled letters
awful suggests something messed up, so the letters of lateness are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone vows to cure their dreadful habit of turning up late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges LATENESS to ESSENTAL, and 'must stop' plugs the I into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential describes something that cannot be done without, a direct synonym of crucially needed.

clue.text: He is one for love, religious type holds

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for

indicators.note: holds means grips inside, so the nun contains the letter for love

parts.note: a nun is a woman in a religious order
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: Someone saying a man of the cloth is in favour of love.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful example: the word 'He' is one of the grammatical items being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: The word he stands in for a noun, so it is an example of this part of speech.

clue.text: Another game rascal with no wife hugs old lady

indicators.note: a hug wraps round, so the shortened rascal goes around the old lady
with no signals that the letter for wife is taken away from the rascal

parts.note: a wretch is a scoundrel or rascal
old lady is slang for mother, MA

explanation.surface: A rogue who has lost his wife embraces his elderly mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' drops W from WRETCH, leaving RETCH, which 'hugs' MA.
explanation.definitionFit: A rematch is a second contest between the same opponents, another game.

clue.text: Bottoms music producers often slapped half-heartedly

indicators.note: the heart of the word is its middle pair of letters, and only half of that pair survives

parts.note: bass guitars, which make music, are often played with a slapping technique

explanation.surface: Bottoms, perhaps of musicians, are spanked half-heartedly.
explanation.walkthrough: BASSES has SS at its heart; 'half-heartedly' loses one S.
explanation.definitionFit: A base is the bottom or foundation of something, so bases are bottoms in that sense.

clue.text: Harry ultimately won't take part in The Shield

indicators.note: the word's last letter refuses to join in, so it is dropped

parts.note: to badger is to harass or harry

explanation.surface: Someone called Harry declines a role in the US police drama The Shield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' is a verb, not a name. In US police slang an officer's badge is called a shield, which the TV series title plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: American police call their metal badge a shield, so the two are the same object.

clue.text: When to go around wandering in Roman republic

indicators.note: going around means turning back on itself, so the short word is read backwards

parts.note: as means when, as in 'as he arrived'

indicators.note: wandering means straying from a set path, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

explanation.surface: A traveller roaming about in ancient Rome's republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go around' turns the short word back to front; 'wandering' shuffles the two words that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny state enclosed by Italy is one of the world's oldest surviving republics.

clue.text: On drugs to shed last bit of unwanted weight

indicators.note: shedding means losing something, so a letter is removed from the drugged word

parts.note: stoned means high on drugs

indicators.note: the final letter of the following word is the one taken

explanation.surface: Someone takes drugs to lose unwanted pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last bit of' picks D from 'unwanted', and 'to shed' takes it off STONED.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone is a British unit of weight equal to fourteen pounds.

clue.text: Smart don's novel that's gritty and violent

indicators.note: novel means new or fresh, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A clever academic has written a book that is tough and brutal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book; it signals rearranging the letters of SMART DON'S.
explanation.definitionFit: A desert storm whips up sand, so it is literally full of grit and fierce in force.

clue.text: Search me flipping naked, but find no drugs? Not likely!

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the shortened naked word is read backwards
find no means a search turns up nothing, so the drugs letter is removed

parts.note: nude means naked
E is slang for ecstasy, so drugs in crosswords
no is a flat refusal, the same as not likely

explanation.surface: A stripped-naked body search turns up no drugs, which seems unlikely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find no' takes E out of NUDE, leaving NUD, and 'flipping' turns that to DUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual replies meaning 'I don't know', so they are interchangeable.

clue.text: Product man on board has son put on head

indicators.note: putting something on the head places it at the front, so the son's letter goes first

parts.note: a pawn is a chess piece, a man on the board

explanation.surface: A man on a company board puts his son at the top of the product team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man on board' is a chessman, not a director.
explanation.definitionFit: Spawn is offspring or something produced, so it means a product in the sense of a result.

clue.text: State where one can see Rooney's tattoos fading

definitions.text: State where one can see Rooney's tattoos
definitions.meaning: footballer Wayne Rooney's tattoos are on Wayne, said the same way as the phrase meant

explanation.surface: Wayne Rooney's ink is losing its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Wayne Rooney is an English footballer; his tattoos are 'on the Wayne', which says the same as the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Something declining in strength is said to be like a moon shrinking, an idiom for fading away.

clue.text: Sex without boundaries? It's a great feeling!

indicators.note: boundaries are the edges, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: relations is a polite word for sex

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic endorsement of uninhibited sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without boundaries' sounds like wild abandon but trims R and S off RELATIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is joy or exhilaration, a great emotional high.

clue.text: Bad loan I'm to readjust from a corporation?

indicators.note: readjusting means setting things up afresh, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A banker plans to restructure a bad loan made by a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' is jocular old slang for a pot belly, not a company.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is old humorous slang for a large belly, so belonging to it is belly-related.

clue.text: Enemy army priest delivered back to front

parts.note: a host is a large army

indicators.note: delivered with back and front swapped means read in reverse

parts.note: Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel

explanation.surface: An enemy force's chaplain is sent back to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enemy' is used as an adjective, as in 'enemy territory'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostile describes an opponent's forces or attitude, matching enemy used as an adjective.

clue.text: Funny bit of ribbing one gives Her Maj?

indicators.note: funny means odd or peculiar, so the letters are put in a strange order
a bit of the word here is its first letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky bit of teasing aimed at the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: R from 'ribbing' joins ONE GIVES, and 'Funny' rearranges the lot. 'Her Maj' is British slang for the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: The reigning monarch, informally Her Majesty, is the country's ruler, so the title fits; the question mark flags it as an example.

clue.text: Complaint I take up following tenant going topless

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the remaining pieces sit after the shortened tenant
losing the top in a down entry means dropping the first letter

parts.note: a renter is a tenant

indicators.note: in a down clue going up reads the word backwards

parts.note: to sit an exam is to take it

explanation.surface: A landlord grumbles about a tenant who goes around topless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going topless' cuts the first letter; in a down entry 'up' reads the word for take backwards. To 'take' an exam is to sit it.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness, and this is inflammation of the intestine.

clue.text: One small row about theologian heading for Lourdes

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the row goes round the other pieces

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
DD is Doctor of Divinity, a theologian

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A short line of pilgrims around a theologian sets off for Lourdes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One small' is the definition: British slang for a little fish or child.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiddler is British slang for a very small fish or young child, a little one.

clue.text: Circus finally gives support to animal trainers

indicators.note: in a down entry a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes after

parts.note: a reebok, or rhebok, is a South African antelope

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A circus act ends by helping its animal handlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trainers' are sports shoes, not handlers.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeboks are a brand of sports shoe, which the British call trainers.

clue.text: Perhaps leave one's castle forever exposed after rook to b4?

indicators.note: after means the exposed piece is placed behind the chess play

parts.note: rook to b4 is a single chess move
out means revealed for good, as when a secret is out

explanation.surface: A chess player warns that shifting a rook will leave their castle open.
explanation.walkthrough: An Englishman's home is his castle, so leaving it is quitting one's house.
explanation.definitionFit: Quitting your home for good is the idiom for changing residence, and the castle here is a house.

clue.text: Clergyman missing his fourth cathedral?

indicators.note: his refers to the clergyman's word, and its fourth letter is the one dropped

parts.note: a minister is a clergyman

explanation.surface: A priest has gone absent from his fourth cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A minster is a large church, often a cathedral, such as York's.

clue.text: Admit Hoskins into company with Conservative slant

indicators.note: into means put inside, so the setter goes in among the company and Conservative letters

parts.note: Hoskins is the setter, who refers to themselves as me
to lean is to slant

explanation.surface: The setter is let into a firm with a right-wing bias.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often name themselves, so 'Hoskins' stands for the first person, as 'me'.
explanation.definitionFit: To confess the truth is an idiom meaning to own up or admit.

clue.text: Short quote about work: "get in loads of trouble!"

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shortened quote goes round the work
short means cut, so the last letter is removed

parts.note: to cite is to quote
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A brief quotation about work warns of a heap of trouble ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' drops the last letter of the word for quote before it wraps around the work.
explanation.definitionFit: This British slang phrase means to be punished or get into serious trouble.

clue.text: Careful, brew leads to riotous yelling

parts.note: cha is British slang for tea, a brew

indicators.note: leads are the front letters, here of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A warning to be careful: making tea can cause a rowdy shouting match.
explanation.definitionFit: Chary means wary or cautious, a synonym of careful.

clue.text: Might one argue with one pulling a blade?

definitions.meaning: someone who has a row, a quarrel, could be called by this word
an oarsman pulls an oar, whose flat end is the blade

explanation.surface: Would someone pick a fight with a person drawing a knife?
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense rhymes with 'power' (from a row, a quarrel); the second with 'grower'.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a quarreller; the other is an oarsman, whose oar ends in a blade.

clue.text: Doctor injecting a bit opium in America, yeah baby!

indicators.note: injecting means putting inside, so the letter goes into the doctor

parts.note: Doctor Who is the British TV time traveller, the Doctor

indicators.note: a bit of the word here is its first letter

explanation.surface: An American cheers as a doctor injects a little opium.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an American cry of delight, like an excited whoop of joy.

clue.text: Briefly sleep around with lawyer (a cuddly-looking bear)

indicators.note: around means turned about, so the short sleep is read backwards

parts.note: a nap is a brief sleep
DA is a District Attorney, a US lawyer

explanation.surface: A lawyer is accused of sleeping around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' sounds like promiscuity but reverses NAP.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda, black and white with a round face, is a bear famed for looking cuddly.

clue.text: Go on strike after unacceptable humour

indicators.note: after means the strike piece is placed behind the other two

parts.note: out means not allowed, as in 'that's out'
wit is humour
to hit is to strike

explanation.surface: Workers walk out after some offensive jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' looks like industrial action but is HIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are urgings to say what you are holding back: 'Go on, tell me'.

clue.text: List everything involved in case for theocracy

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped inside, so everything goes into the outer letters
the case of a word is its outer letters, the first and last

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: A list of everything bearing on the argument for religious rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A tally is a running count or record, which serves as a list.

clue.text: Sadly almost used to runs requiring much effort

indicators.note: sadly means badly or regrettably, so the letters are put out of order
almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone who sadly has nearly got used to going for runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts USED to USE; 'Sadly' rearranges USE, TO and RUNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Strenuous means arduous, needing great exertion.
